title: Catalysts and equilibrium
subtitle: Sooner product, or more at equilibrium?
subject: Chemistry
syllabusDotPoints: Candidate C-activation explanation subset. Investigation, practical conduct and complete syllabus-action coverage remain pending.
inquiryQuestion: Why does a catalyst change reaction speed without changing equilibrium composition?
lessonIntent: Explain the lower alternative pathway, faster approach and unchanged fixed-temperature equilibrium composition and K under matching conditions.
examSkill: Distinguish product formed in a limited time from the equilibrium amount.

scenes.heading: Sooner, or more at equilibrium?
scenes.body:
Sooner product?
More product at equilibrium?

voiceover.text: A catalyst can make product appear sooner. Does that mean there will be more product when equilibrium is reached? Those are two different questions: how fast we get there, and what mixture we finish with.

scenes.heading: Another pathway, a lower hurdle
scenes.body:
Energy versus reaction progress
Schematic exothermic example

voiceover.text: Activation energy is the energy hurdle for a reaction pathway. On this diagram, the vertical axis shows energy. The horizontal axis follows progress along the reaction pathway, not time. A catalyst provides another pathway with a lower hurdle. That reversible pathway helps the forward and reverse reactions. It does not change the energies of the starting substances and products.

scenes.heading: The equilibrium relationship stays fixed
scenes.body:
K: the equilibrium concentration relationship
Same temperature: same K

voiceover.text: The equilibrium constant, K, describes the equilibrium concentration relationship for this reaction. As in the temperature lesson, its value stays the same when the temperature stays the same. The catalyst changes the pathway, not that equilibrium relationship.

scenes.heading: A faster approach to the same mixture
scenes.body:
Same reacting amounts and starting composition
Same fixed volume and temperature
Initially forming product

voiceover.text: If the mixture is still approaching equilibrium, the catalyst lets it approach faster. Compare mixtures with the same starting amounts and composition, container volume and temperature. We start with a mixture forming product. The graph shows its product concentration rising towards the same equilibrium level, with a faster approach when a catalyst is present. These curves are schematic, not measured times.

scenes.heading: Already at equilibrium?
scenes.body:
Forward reaction forms product
Reverse reaction uses product
At equilibrium: equal rates, no net change

voiceover.text: If it is already at equilibrium, both directions continue with equal rates through the catalysed system. There is no net shift. Faster forward and reverse reactions do not mean that product keeps building up: one direction forms it while the other uses it.

scenes.heading: Compare two matching mixtures
scenes.body:
Two closed mixtures: same reacting amounts and starting composition
Same container volume and temperature; initially forming product
Only one mixture has a catalyst
Could it contain more product before both reach equilibrium?
Could it contain more after both reach equilibrium? Explain.

voiceover.text: Two closed mixtures start with the same reacting amounts and composition, in the same container volume at the same temperature. Both are initially forming product as they approach equilibrium. Only one has a catalyst. Could it contain more product before both reach equilibrium? Could it contain more after both reach equilibrium? Explain the difference.

scenes.heading: Separate time from equilibrium amount
scenes.body:
Earlier: more product can be present
At equilibrium: same composition

voiceover.text: It can contain more product earlier if the starting mixture is forming product as it approaches equilibrium. But after both reach equilibrium, their composition is the same. Faster production during a limited time is different from a larger equilibrium amount.

scenes.heading: Key notes: what to write in your book
scenes.body:
Catalyst: lower-energy alternative pathway, assisting both directions.
Same reacting amounts, starting composition, volume and temperature: faster approach, same equilibrium composition and K.
More product in a limited time can mean faster production, not more at equilibrium.

voiceover.text: You can copy this short distinction for your book. Pause if you need longer.

points: Catalyst: lower-energy alternative pathway, assisting both directions.
Same reacting amounts, starting composition, volume and temperature: faster approach, same equilibrium composition and K.
More product in a limited time can mean faster production, not more at equilibrium.
